newsitem.title: USA: U.S's Thompson undeterred by uncooperative witnesses.
newsitem.headline: U.S's Thompson undeterred by uncooperative witnesses.

text.p: The chairman of the U.S. Senate panel that opens hearings this week into political fund-raising scandals said on Sunday said he is undeterred by the lack of cooperation two key figures are giving his investigation.

Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson said he can conduct a successful investigation without the testimony of former Commerce Department official John Huang or Charles Yah Lin Trie, a former Arkansas restaurant owner and longtime friend of President Bill Clinton.

"I think it's important that the committee lay out the facts that it can, give depth and perception, the facts that are already on the record, and paint a picture," Thompson said on the "ABC This Week" television programme.

"And Sam Ervin used to say that if you could paint a real good picture of a cow, you didn't need to write the word 'cow' under it," he said, invoking the name of the North Carolina Democrat who chaired the 1973 Senate Watergate hearings on which Thompson served as Republican counsel.

Huang, who later moved to the Democratic National Committee, has made clear he would invoke the Fifth Amendment against self-incrimination if called to testify. Trie, who lives in China now, has said he would refuse to testify.
The two men raised nearly $4 million from Asian-American sources but the DNC has returned $1.6 million in questionable contributions raised by Huang and $645,000 donated or raised by Trie.

Thompson, who has insisted that the probe would examine campaign finance issues of Republicans as well as Democrats, said more subpoenas will be issued this week, but declined to say who the first witnesses are likely to be on Wednesday after the hearings begin an expected full day of opening statements on Tuesday.
But he said the hearings would focus initially on whether Chinese officials sought to influence U.S. foreign policy with campaign contributions.
"That'll certainly be a big part of it, and that'll certainly be a part of the first section that we address," he said.

Thompson said he asked U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last week to assist his panel in some ways, including providing with information, but declined to say whether he asked her to help convince China to return Trie to the United States so he could testify.
"We've asked for several things, frankly," he said. "There's other information besides witnesses."

Saying he was concerned about the length of time it was taking the U.S. Justice Department to respond to committee requests for grants of immunity from prosecution for some witnesses, Thompson said he is prepared to seek an extension of his investigation beyond its year-end expiration, if its work is unfinished.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said he favoured using immunity grants to gain the testimony of certain witnesses. "Finding out what happened is far more important than sending people to jail," he said on the CBS News programme, "Face the Nation."
